title: The Zohar's companions on the road
hookLine: the Zohar's sages walk the roads of Galilee, teaching as they go
carry: where companions talk torah, the presence walks along

cards: Two rabbis are walking on a road. Dust, heat, hills, a long way still to go. One says to the other: let's open our mouths with words of Torah, so the walk isn't wasted.

An old man trudges along with them, driving a donkey, a hired hand as far as they can tell. Then the donkey driver starts to talk, and out of his mouth come teachings that leave the two rabbis astonished.
The Zohar, a central book of Kabbalah, tells scenes like this. Here, the teaching happens on the road.

teach.b: Companions on the road. In Aramaic, the Zohar calls them the chevraya, the companions. First, who they are.
Tradition ties the Zohar to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, a sage of the Mishnah, and the book tells of him and his circle walking the roads of the land of Israel, Galilee and beyond, teaching as they go.
Scholars ask hard questions about when the book was written, and there are different answers. Either way, inside the book, this is the scene: friends, walking, talking Torah. Second, why the road.
Yesterday: when people sit together and their talk is Torah, the Shechinah rests among them.
The Zohar's companions carry that onto the road; its sages say that when travelers speak words of Torah, the presence joins them on the way. A road becomes a moving sanctuary.

Third, the stranger. More than once in the Zohar, the teacher turns out to be someone the companions overlooked: an old donkey driver, a child, a traveler on the road. Wisdom may be walking just behind them.
In these stories, nobody learns alone.
One companion asks a question, another answers, a third sees something new in the answer, and Rabbi Shimon praises them when they get it right.
The secrets of the Torah, in this picture, open up between people, in conversation, on the way somewhere.

how: The Zohar is often studied in pairs or small circles, reading aloud together, and some study groups take walks or journeys to sites in Galilee linked to its sages.

games.q: what does “companions on the road” mean?
o: students who studied only inside a closed hall
the Zohar's circle of friends, teaching as they walk
pilgrims walking up to the Temple for a festival

games.q: companions on the road — tap the pairs.
p: the sage tradition ties to the Zohar

s: in the Zohar, teaching happens only in a study hall
the companions teach as they walk the roads.
the deepest teacher in a Zohar scene can be a donkey driver
someone the companions overlooked turns out to be the teacher.
the Zohar's sages learn alone, in silence
nobody learns alone: one asks, another answers, a third sees more.

games.q: you're one of two rabbis on a dusty road. a donkey driver trudges behind you. what does the Zohar's story do with him?
o: he stays silent all the way.
he turns out to be a great teacher.
games.why: he opens his mouth and teaches things that leave the rabbis astonished. wisdom was walking just behind them.

practice: Think of one person you'd like to walk beside, a friend, a sibling, someone you've lost touch with, and picture the road and the ground under your feet.
Then hold one real question you'd want to ask them, not small talk, something about what matters to them, and keep the question and their face together for a while.

wordCard.voice: Companions on the road. The chevraya of the Zohar: friends walking together, teaching Torah as they go, and finding wisdom in strangers. Today's words.

orig.note: Aramaic: the companions, the Zohar's name for Rabbi Shimon's circle.

carryVoice: Your line: where companions talk torah, the presence walks along. The book itself teaches like a walk with friends. Rest well.
